title: What a founder should ask in the first studio call
metaTitle: Questions for the first studio call
excerpt: On a first studio call, ask who does the work, what you will own, how decisions get made, and what done looks like. A pleasant conversation is not a substitute for those answers.
primaryKeyword: questions to ask a design studio
alt: A white wall covered with framed prints, small plants, and two floating shelves, a room you can read before you decide whether to sit down.
caption: A wall you can read before you sit. The first studio call should be that clear. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a founder ask on the first call with a design studio?
faqs.answer: Ask who will design and build the work, what you will own at the end, how a decision gets made, and what done looks like in pages and states. Chemistry can be real. It does not replace those four answers.

faqs.question: What should the client own when a site project ends?
faqs.answer: The repository, the domain, the hosting and content logins, the design files, and the licenses for type and photographs. Accounts should be in the client's name. A project that lives only inside a vendor login is hard to leave.

faqs.question: How should a studio define done?
faqs.answer: Done is a list of pages and states, including empty, error, and the phone view, plus a way for the client to edit the words that change. A walkthrough of a design file is not the same thing as using the site. Ask what is deliberately out of the release.

markdown:
The first call with a studio should answer four things. Who will do the work. What you will own when it is finished. How decisions get made. What done looks like. Questions to ask a design studio are those four, asked in plain language, before chemistry convinces you to skip them.

Chemistry matters. You are going to be in a working relationship. It is not a substitute for the answers. A pleasant hour that leaves ownership vague is an expensive hour.

## Who actually does the work

Ask who will design, who will build, and who will be in the room with you. Names are better than a headcount. A founder needs to know whether the people on the call are the people on the project.

Ask what happens when someone is away. A small studio should be able to say how the work continues. A large studio should be able to say whether your project is staffed by the people who sold it. Either model can be honest. The dishonest version is a senior conversation followed by a silent handoff.

Ask what they do themselves and what they subcontract. Illustration, photography, copy, and specialized engineering are often shared with other people. That can be a strength. You should hear it now, including how those people are directed and whether you will meet them.

Google's helpful-content guidance puts weight on who created something, and treats trust as the center of experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness. A marketing site can dodge that question. Your project should not. If a studio cannot say who makes the work, you cannot judge the trust you are about to buy.

Hanabi is a studio that designs and builds. The relevant version of this question, asked of us or of anyone else, is which parts are in the room and which are not. Stack names are a clue, not a credential. Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, Motion, Prisma, PostgreSQL, and Vercel are tools. The question is whether the same team that chooses them will be accountable for the page a customer touches.

## What you will own

Ask for a list. The repository. The domain and the DNS. The hosting account. The content logins. The design files. The type and the logo in a form you can reuse. Analytics. The ad accounts, if any. The store admin, if you sell online.

Ask whose names are on the accounts on day one. A studio can help you open them. The accounts should be yours. A project that lives only inside a vendor login is a project you cannot leave.

Ask about the files after delivery. On a Hanabi project the client portal holds brand files, docs, and updates. That is one concrete answer. Whatever the studio's answer is, it should name a place, not "we'll send a zip." A zip in a chat is how logos go missing.

Ask about the fonts, photographs, and code licenses. What you can use on the next campaign. What you must not use. A beautiful site with a type license that expires, or a photograph you do not have rights to, is a later invoice.

Ask what they keep. Studios keep the right to show public work. That is normal. Ask what stays private. Unreleased product, numbers, and customer data should have a clear line. If you do not want a project in a portfolio, say so before the contract, not after the launch post.

## How decisions get made

Ask who can approve, on their side and on yours. A call that flatters every stakeholder and names no decider will stall in week three. You need a single owner on your side who can say yes, and a single owner on theirs who can say what the yes costs.

Ask how a change is judged. A new page idea during a build is either a swap for something in scope, or a later phase. Hope is not a process. The studio should be able to describe the difference without drama. You should be able to hear it without feeling managed.

Ask what the working rhythm is. A weekly review of real pages beats a monthly reveal of a slide. Ask what you need to bring to each review. Copy, access, a decision, a constraint. Studios stall when the founder disappears and then rewrites the work in one late email. You can ask the studio how they handle that. You should also decide that you will show up.

Ask how disagreement works. If they think your headline is wrong, will they say so? A studio that only agrees is a pair of hands. A studio that cannot explain the disagreement is a lecture. You want the version that shows the trade and lets you choose.

Figma is where many of those choices should be visible. Comments, a named frame, a decision written on it. Framer can show a flow when motion or sequence is the question. Neither tool is the decision. The decision is a sentence in the notes: we chose this, and we left that out.

## What done looks like

Ask for done in objects. These pages. These states. Empty, error, loading, and the one awkward edge case you already know about. The forms. The basic metadata. A CMS path your team can use. Analytics that record the action you care about. A launch list.

Ask what done does not include. A brand film. A full design system for a company that needed a site. Twelve social templates. Ongoing marketing. If those matter, they can be a phase. They should not be assumed inside the word "website."

Ask how quality will be checked. A walkthrough of a Figma file is not the same as using the site on a phone. Design QA belongs on the real pages. Core Web Vitals, readable type, and a form that can be finished are part of a serious launch. You do not need to recite metrics on the call. You need to hear that someone will open the site on a phone before you announce it.

Ask what you receive on the last day besides the URL. Access, the repo, the files, a short note on how to edit the things that change, and a list of what is deliberately unfinished. A launch without that list becomes a quarrel about memory.

Public work is a way to test their answer. Down the Cove, Thomas Bewick, Ballarat Box Sports, Wabisabi, Got Next, Leadly, and Trade Moai are projects Hanabi can point at. Asked of any studio, the question is the same: show a project and say what done meant on that one. A gallery with no sentence about the constraint is not an answer.

## Money, time, and the shape of the engagement

Ask how they price, in the shape, not as a dare. Fixed scope fits a known set of pages and states. An ongoing engagement fits a product that will keep changing. Ask which one they think you are, and why. A studio that only sells one shape will bend your project to fit it.

Ask what a change costs in process, even if the number comes later in a proposal. You are listening for whether a change is discussable. A room that cannot talk about a swap will surprise you later.

Ask what they need from you in the first two weeks. Access, a decision-maker, existing analytics, the words you are willing to say. If you cannot provide those, the schedule they quote is fiction. Say so on the call.

Ask what happens if you pause. Ownership should not depend on a retainer. You should be able to keep the repo and the accounts if the work stops. A pause can end the service. It should not end your ability to publish.

You do not need a detailed timeline from a first call. You do need to hear whether they think in weeks of review or in a single reveal. Those are different risks.

## A call is a sample of the work

Notice how they listen. A good studio asks what the offer is, who it is for, and what is already true. A weak one presents a process diagram before you have finished the sentence. Process can be real. It should arrive after the problem.

Notice whether they invent certainty. No honest studio knows your conversion rate, your launch date, or your revenue after one call. They can know the shape of a first release. Be wary of a guarantee that your market has not earned.

Notice the questions they ask you. You are also being evaluated. If they do not ask who decides, what you will provide, and what the offer is, the project will start without those answers anyway, and you will pay for the discovery in rework.

Bring artifacts. The current site, the deck you send to customers, a product screenshot, the sentence you wish were true. A call with nothing to look at becomes a conversation about taste. Taste is part of the work. It is a poor agenda for the first meeting.

The portfolio is the other half of this evaluation. Chemistry on a call can be real and the work can still be vague. The piece on [how to read a studio portfolio](/blog/how-to-read-a-studio-portfolio) is the next read, so you know what to look for before you are charmed by the frames.

When you are ready to ask these questions of Hanabi, start with [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) so you can see the shape of the work, then bring the four questions to the first conversation. Who does it. What you own. How a decision is made. What done is.
